Thank you, co-lead. Mutual administrative assistance is the backbone of effective international tax cooperation. For countries like ours, it is a practical necessity to safeguard domestic revenues, strengthen compliance, and ensure that taxation supports sustainable development rather than being undermined by evasion and aggressive avoidance. Ghana fully aligns with the statement delivered by Zambia on behalf of the Africa group. We share the view that Article 9 is central to the credibility and effectiveness of this instrument, particularly in enabling developing countries to participate on an equal footing in cross-border taxation cooperation. At the same time, we take note of the concerns raised by India, St. Kitts and Nevis and others regarding the reference to the widest measure possible, as well as the proposals reflected in paragraph three. These concerns underscore the need for clarity, balance and practicality in implementation while preserving the core objective of a meaningful cooperation. Ghana wishes to briefly comment on the formulation in paragraph one, referring to facilitating the effective assessment of taxes. While we fully support the objective of strengthening tax assessment, the use of the word effective may be problematic. It is inherently subjective and may be interpreted differently across jurisdictions. and could inadvertently introduce a results-based standard rather than an obligation of cooperation. From Ghana's perspective, these risks creating asymmetries in the implementation and conditioning assistance on capacity or outcomes contrary to the spirit of inclusive international tax cooperation. We therefore believe that language focusing on facilitation and cooperation without subjective qualifiers would provide greater legal certainty and better reflect the realities of developing countries on tax administration. Ghana also looks favorably on Nigeria's proposal to replace the word assessment with administration in paragraph one. Ghana strongly supports the Africa group's proposal on paragraph three. Recognizing guidance or additional instruments to be provided by the Conference of Parties is essential. It allows the framework to evolve, respond to capacity constraints, and ensure that mutual administrative assistance is implemented in a manner that is effective, coordinated, and sensitive to the diverse realities of our administrations. In conclusion, Article 9 must remain ambitious yet workable, By anchoring its implementation in collective guidance agreed by state parties, we can ensure that mutual administrative assistance truly delivers on its promise for Africa and for all. We also acknowledge

However,

It is equally important to acknowledge that these instruments are not yet sufficient in practice to fully meet the objectives we collectively seek to achieve here.

As highlighted during the intervention by Germany, assistance in the collection of taxes is a critical enabler for achieving domestic resource mobilization goals, particularly for developing countries, but also for developed economies. Tax audits and substantive principles in the absence of an effective and workable mechanism for collection have limited practical utility. In this context, it is essential that we re-examine existing conventions and identify loopholes that act as barriers to effective mutual assistance. The objective is not duplication of existing instruments but refinement of current provisions so that they can function more effectively and serve their intended purpose. Considering the discussions held so far and the shared understanding emerging from the room, India proposes the following language for consideration for this particular Article 9. I would read it as follows, state parties shall afford one another mutual administrative assistance in tax matters to facilitate the effective administration and enforcement of tax matters to combat tax evasion and avoidance through various measures as may be agreed by the State Parties through protocols or other instruments. State Parties shall cooperate to identify and eliminate administrative barriers that prevent effective mutual administrative assistance in tax matters without compromising procedural safeguards. We would share this proposal in writing on the informal channel also. The proposed language is intended to strike a careful and necessary balance between effectiveness and safeguards in the area of mutual administrative assistance in tax matters. Secondly, the reference to various measures as may be agreed by the state parties through protocols or other instruments. provides the required flexibility and this is in alignment with the interventions made by Nigeria, Zambia and other countries of the African group. It allows states to tailor the scope, modalities and depth of assistance in accordance with their domestic legal framework, capacities and evolving international best practices and thus enabling progressive development of cooperation over time. Thirdly, the provision calling upon state parties to cooperate to identify and eliminate administrative barriers, response directly to the practical experience of many countries where existing legal or procedural obstacles limit the effectiveness of mutual assistance. Addressing such barriers is essential to ensure that cooperation is not merely theoretical, but operational and result oriented. At the same time, the language explicitly safeguards procedural protections by clarifying that the elimination of administrative barriers shall not come at the expense of procedural safeguards, which ensures there is a due respect for the process, confidentiality, taxpayer rights, domestic legal principles, and addressing the concerns of several delegates on this matter. The proposed text is not aimed at expanding obligations indiscriminately, but at enhancing the effectiveness of existing cooperation frameworks while preserving core safeguards. Submitted, please. You are all well aware that country-by-country reports are central to curbing aggressive tax planning by multinational corporations. They cover each jurisdiction in which a company operates, including where subsidiaries are located and where they have operations, income, employees, assets, sales, and taxes are paid. Country by country reporting was introduced in the BEPS framework, but the information is protected by fiscal secrecy and confidentiality, and developing countries struggle to get access to that information, which they do not receive from an automatic exchange of information in which they do not participate. Similar reporting mechanisms are currently being introduced within the European Union and Australia. But because access to information exchange remains limited and public data is highly aggregated, most developing countries have little or no access to these reports. I also want to take the opportunity as a representative of a human rights organization to make some points on transparency and rights. Under international human rights law, corporations are not rights holders. As for individuals, no right is absolute, and this includes privacy. The extent to which the right to privacy is protected depends on how it impacts other rights. In tax matters, tax transparency is essential to protect economic and social rights of the majority of the population. At the same time, privacy and secrecy are not the same.
